rationale: B wins because it knows when three angles are enough: “Airbnb wants the corporate travel budget, and it's routing the expenses through Concur and Ramp” turns the supplied dashboard, billing, and integration facts into one beat-specific channel story. A is useful, but “Airbnb's New Business-Ready Badge Asks Hosts to Upgrade. Many Won't Qualify.” asserts the missing proof in the headline, then asks for that proof later. That is the difference between a disciplined angle set and a smart set that still needs adult supervision.
gaps_in_A: “Many Won't Qualify” is not in the facts. The set later admits it needs data on how many hosts qualify, so the headline is overclaiming.
“Targeting the Market Navan Built” and the list “Navan, TravelPerk, Booking.com for Business” add competitor context not supplied in the update. Useful if sourced, lazy if not.
“Ramp has been a fast-growing player in corporate expense management” is outside the fact block and unnecessary to make the integration angle work.
“the compliance gap that blocked corporate adoption” turns a plausible obstacle into established history without evidence.
gaps_in_B: “off a small base it won't size” implies Airbnb refused to provide the denominator. The fact block only says the base is small; it does not say Airbnb withheld it.
“hotelization of home-sharing” is a sharp frame, but it needs host data or analyst support before it becomes more than a tidy wrapper.

“expense rails that managed corporate travel runs on” is directionally plausible, but still depends on what the Concur and Ramp integrations actually do. Good set, but that phrase is carrying weight the facts have not earned yet.
The next step, “journalist-fit-check,” is slightly out of order without names. Pick the angle, gather the missing proof, then build and fit-check the list.
